Evidence & Reading · Critical Appraisal

How We Know

Every clinical claim in this library is stored next to the source's own words. This page opens that ledger — including the places where we got it wrong and had to correct it.

If you only take one thing from this page: a citation is not evidence. A paper can be real, peer-reviewed, correctly formatted and still not contain the number someone attributed to it.

The ledger, at a glance

Every source in evidence_annotations.json stores a verbatim span — the sentence the paper itself wrote — and the claim our teaching pages make from it. A validator refuses the build if a claim has no span, or if a positively-worded claim is licensed by a null or negative one.

What the evidence actually looks like

Each claim is tagged by the direction of what the paper found. Notice how small the cleanly positive slice is — this is the honest shape of a clinical literature, and it is the single best argument against reading only abstracts and conclusions.

Mixed — 17 Positive — 14 Descriptive — 9 Negative — 6

Only 14 of 46 claims report a clean positive finding. The largest group is mixed — the paper found something, and also found a reason to doubt it. Copy that drops the second half is where most citation errors are born.

Correction 1 — The paper that had no number in it

Caught in faculty review · 2026-08-24

Modini et al. (PMID 41664893) is a viewpoint — an argument about how the field should study post-discharge risk. It reports no time-course statistic of its own. It was cited for one at four places in the library. The worst of the four was a quiz answer, which is the version students actually memorise.

What the library saidA post-discharge time-course figure, attributed to Modini.
Research has repeatedly failed to account for the high suicide rate post-discharge from a psychiatric hospital. It is apparent that research in this field largely focuses on simple categorical variables and fails to consider inpatient experiences of their admission and treatment. Empirically investigating how the treatment experience itself can contribute to post-discharge adverse outcomes is required. modini-large-2026 · PMID 41664893 · DOI 10.1177/10398562261425069 · span: abstract · retrieved 2026-08-23 — a critique of the literature, not a measurement of it. There is no rate in this paragraph.

The fix. The claim was re-sourced to two papers that do carry the figures, both verified against PubMed before use:

chung-2017-postdischarge-suicide · PMID 28564699Pooled across 100 studies, the post-discharge suicide rate was 484 per 100 000 person-years overall, 1132 within 3 months after discharge and 2078 among patients admitted with suicidal ideas or behaviors, with rates remaining high for many years after discharge.
chung-2019-first-week-month · PMID 30904843The pooled suicide rate was 2950 per 100 000 person years in the first week and 2060 in the first month after psychiatric hospitalisation, acknowledging marked heterogeneity and evidence of publication bias towards papers reporting a higher rate of postdischarge suicide.

Why the automated check missed it. PubMed types Modini as "Journal Article", not "Editorial", so an article-type filter is blind to it. And the claim carried no numeral of its own, so a numeric-assertion trigger never fired. A person reading the paper caught this. That is not a failure of the tooling — it is the boundary of it.

Correction 2 — The numbers were right and the sentence was still wrong

Caught in faculty review · 2026-08-24

The library described psychoeducation in schizophrenia as having "the strongest evidence base of any single psychological intervention." The effect sizes quoted alongside it were accurate. The superlative was not — and it sat directly beside the Cochrane reviewers' own warning about the quality of the studies producing it.

What the library saidRelapse RR 0.70 (NNT 9); readmission RR 0.71 (NNT 5) — "the strongest evidence base of any single psychological intervention."
Relapse appeared to be lower in psychoeducation group (n = 1214, RR 0.70 CI 0.61 to 0.81, NNT 9 CI 7 to 14) and this also applied to readmission (n = 206, RR 0.71 CI 0.56 to 0.89, NNT 5 CI 4 to 13). Psychoeducation does seem to reduce relapse, readmission and encourage medication compliance, as well as reduce the length of hospital stay in these hospital-based studies of limited quality. The true size of effect is likely to be less than demonstrated in this review - but, nevertheless, some sort of psychoeducation could be clinically effective and potentially cost beneficial. xia-2011 · PMID 21678337 · DOI 10.1002/14651858.CD002831.pub2 · span: abstract · retrieved 2026-08-23 — the reviewers' own limits sit in the same paragraph as the effect sizes.

The fix. The claim now says what the paper says:

xia-2011 · PMID 21678337Psychoeducation in schizophrenia reduced relapse (NNT 9) and readmission (NNT 5), on hospital-based studies of limited quality whose true size of effect is likely to be less than demonstrated in the review.

Three facts the original copy had dropped were added back: the readmission estimate rests on n = 206 of 5,142 participants, the reviewers' own quality caveat, and the fact that the last search was run in 2010. Nothing about the numbers changed. What changed is that the sentence now says what the paper says.

The rules this library holds itself to

1

Every claim carries the source's own words.

A sentence asserting what a paper found must ship with that paper's verbatim span in the same change. No span, no build.

2

Read the results, not the title or the conclusion.

A review pass found that a majority of early annotations needed amendment, and a handful said close to the opposite of the paper — all of them written from titles.

3

When claim and paper disagree, the claim is what changes.

The stored policy is explicit: "Rewrite the claim to match the paper. Do not edit the span, and do not move the claim to a paper that does not support it." Trimming the inconvenient half of a quotation is the error, not the fix.

4

Evidence expires.

A span older than the policy's maximum age must be re-verified against the source before the claim it licenses can keep standing.

5

The backlog may only shrink.

Sources that predate this gate are listed by name in the file and are still unverified. Nothing may be added to that list — it is a debt register, not a loophole.

Your turn

Here is a verbatim span. Which claim does it license?

The pooled estimate of the suicide rate in the first month postdischarge suicide was 2060 per 100 000 person years (95% CI=1300 to 3280, I2=90). The pooled estimate of the suicide rate in the first week postdischarge suicide was 2950 suicides per 100 000 person years (95% CI=1740 to 5000, I2=88). Eight studies that were included after personal communication had lower pooled rates of suicide than studies included after data extraction and there was evidence of publication bias towards papers reporting a higher rate of postdischarge suicide. Acknowledging the presence of marked heterogeneity between studies and the likelihood of bias towards publication of studies reporting a higher postdischarge suicide rate, the first week and first month postdischarge following psychiatric hospitalisation are periods of extraordinary suicide risk. chung-2019-first-week-month · PMID 30904843 · DOI 10.1136/bmjopen-2018-023883 · span: abstract · retrieved 2026-08-24
